#2037. Gasly takes shock Italian GP pole and denies Russell

Sometimes inspiration can come from the unlikeliest of sources. After claiming the first pole of his Formula One career, an absolutely stunning effort in his 192nd attempt – edging out Mercedes’ George Russell right at the death – Alpine’s Pierre Gasly revealed that a harmless jibe from his performance coach Ben Thorpe just before the session started had riled him up.

It turned out Gasly and Russell had been playing online chess until about 15 minutes before qualifying.

“Since the [drivers’] briefing last night, I figured out that he [Russell] is obsessed with chess, and so am I,” Gasly explained later in his press conference. “There are a few of us in the paddock who are. So we have exchanged our IDs on Chess.com and we have had a little game going on.

“I won yesterday, and another one that carried on into today,” the Frenchman added. “I was feeling confident and I was picking [taking] piece after piece. Then Ben told me: ‘You are getting George here but he is going to get you in a few minutes!’. And I thought ‘F--- off!’.”

What a way to break your duck. And what a day on which to do it. On Friday, Gasly lost his only podium of the season when the International Court of Appeal reinstated two five-second penalties he received in Monaco, dropping him from third to seventh in that race. The ruling produced fireworks when Flavio Briatore, Alpine’s executive adviser, then accused one of the judges on the ICA panel of being biased towards McLaren, one of two teams who had brought the appeal.

Another 24 hours later, the fireworks were for all the right reasons. And there was no appealing the result; the start of Russell’s final lap in Q3 was slightly compromised by Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, but the Englishman could have no real complaints, losing out by 0.060secs in the end, prompting wild celebrations in the Alpine garage.

To say the result was a surprise would be an understatement. This was the Enstone team’s first pole in 17 years, since Fernando Alonso took P1 Renault at the 2009 Hungarian Grand Prix.

The warning signs were there. Alpine had been quick all weekend. But the Tifosi packing Monza’s grandstands fully expected it to be a battle between Mercedes and their beloved Ferrari for pole.

The Scuderia’s performance was underwhelming. Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton were only ninth and 10th quickest in Q2, the latter squeaking into Q3 by one thousandth of a second from Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto. “F--- me,” Hamilton said after dodging that bullet.

And although they improved a bit in Q3, Hamilton managing to claim P5, just behind Leclerc in P4, they never threatened the front row. In fact, they later got lucky as McLaren’s Oscar Piastri, who took P3, was later hit with a three-place grid drop post-qualifying for impeding Liam Lawson, meaning both Ferrari drivers rose one place.

It could prove significant. Hamilton, like Russell, knows this weekend represents a golden opportunity to close the gap to Kimi Antonelli in the title race. The two Britons are tied second in the championship heading into the weekend, 59 points behind the Italian. But Antonelli, who sacrificed his qualifying to help Russell, must start from the back of the grid on Sunday due to exceeding the permitted number of engines in a season.

It promises to be a fascinating race, with Antonelli fighting his way through the pack and Russell and Hamilton trying to make hay while they can. Russell sounded confident. “I think they [Alpine] have got a car that’s got some good straight-line speed, which will be nice for them in the race. But, yeah, confident I’ve got the pace to go for the win.”

Could he be underestimating Gasly again? The Frenchman, who lives locally in Milan and speaks fluent Italian, has won here before. He claimed the only victory of his F1 career at Monza for AlphaTauri in 2020.

“Anything is possible tomorrow,” insisted Steve Nielsen, Alpine’s managing director. “We didn’t expect to be in pole position, we are. Tomorrow, good starts, good strategy, good pit stops – who knows? Let’s try to win it.”

Gasly himself said he had no idea what he was capable of. “My plan is to stay first as long as I can. How long is that going to be? I have no idea. My focus is going to be on my driving and making no mistakes and making the best out of what I have.” Perhaps that will be enough for another checkmate.

Antonelli acknowledged that his engine-parts grid penalty meant he had no reason not to assist his teamate Russell by offering towing assistance.

He seemed a little peeved at times on the radio, but he did his job. With Russell likely to need to return the favour for him later this season, there is no point causing bother.

He told Sky Sports: “It’s what I have to do. The team asked me and of course I did what I had to do, I tried to help as much as possible. It’s a bit weird going in two, even the lap I did alone was a bit of a weird feeling. Overall with the penalty today I had to be a good teammate and I had to help as much as I could. I think I did a good job with that and happy it worked out.”

Here’s Oscar Piastri, asked if a pole had been possible: “I don’t think so, no. I think the first lap felt good and I tried to see if anyone wanted to go in front out of the pit lane but no one did and I knew it was always going to be difficult and misjudged the braking a little bit and locked up. That was the session but good to have a decent result, it has been a while. I’ll take it.”

Alpine managing director Steve Nielsen said to Sky Sports that they were aiming high: “Pierre is a class act, as you say, if you give him the machine, he will deliver. We failed to do that a few times last year. We haven’t always given him the most competitive machinery this year, but when we have he has delivered. Particularly earlier in the season so to see the team bounce back, to see him deliver on the track he knows well, he lives locally, he lives in Milan. It was wonderful.

“We mustn’t forget Franco either, he’s done a great job today. I really feel we have given them a good car, and who knows? Anything is possible tomorrow.”

Here’s what he said immediately after the session: “Massive congrats to Pierre because that’s an incredible performance. We were actually playing a game of chess about 15 minutes before qualifying and he beat me there and I thought ‘well I think I’ll beat you in qualifying’ and here we are - he’s ahead of me again! I was disappointed not to get pole. It was a bit messy with Verstappen opening the lap. But Pierre and Alpine have been super fast, even from Q1. Happy to see them get a good result.”

Gasly’s advantage, it appears, seems to be over Russell’s car understeering and lacking grip in turbulent air.

P1 ☝️#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/U0hebWsjWY

He says: “It was amazing, thank you everyone. It was an incredible qualy. I felt very good in the car. I was trying to chip away in evert session. I’m so happy, it’s been nine years trying to get a pole. First win [was] in Monza, to get pole is very special.”

He then pays credit to his team and the fans in Italian, and I am leaning on my Latin to get the gist of it.

“I was disappointed not to get the pole,” admits Russell who said he had been playing chess with Gasly before the game and the Frenchman won that, with Russell confident he was going to beat him in qualifying.

Alpine been in the news all weekend. Fair to say that pole lap from Gasly is better PR for the team than Flavio Briatore’s bizarre outburst in the FIA press conference yesterday. Well done that man.

His tone is evidently disappointed. In truth, given Hamilton is fifth, he is in a strong position to have the best of the weekend.

Gasly, yes, was fastest, but Russell has been the most consistent.

Piastri could be in trouble, too, for impeding earlier in the day’s sesion. Ferrari, in fourth and fifth, do not look entirely competitive.

Russell is second, Piastri third, Leclerc fourth, Hamilton fifth, Verstappen sixth, Antonelli seventh, Colapinto eighth, Norris ninth and Lindblad 10th.

He starts his flying lap, and locks up at turn 1 and exceeds track limits. That means Norris will be unable to get a tow from him too.

After being the quickest at FP2 and FP3, he is top of the pack once more with a bit over five minutes left.

Antonelli has done him a favour there, but Russell may need to return the favour in similar circumstances down the line.

Hamilton is now down in ninth, and struggling, about 0.8s off the pace.

Hamilton needs to catch Leclerc to get a tow. It failed to happen last time out.

Piastri finished Q2 in P2 but it looks likely he'll be penalised for this incident involving Lawson#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/RGzzEeqyql

Lawson, Hulkenberg, Sainz, Ocon, Bearman and Bortoleto are all out.

Hamilton is 10th, one-thousandth of a second quick enough to scrape through, and Leclrec ninth.

“**** me” exclaims Hamilton, without saying, ‘Asterisk’ once.

Antonelli asks for the chance to go out with another team ahead so he can get a tow of his own.

Norris now second quickest, so perhaps those brakes are up to speed.

There is some suggestion that Hamilton might need a front wing change.

The Silver Arrows working in tandem Kimi in front, George slipstreaming behind #F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/H476E91GJs

But Gasly is going fastest in his out lap.

Verstappen now goes fastest. Lawson is in behind, with Carlos Sainz making a surprise appearance up top.

Hamilton and Russell are yet to lay down times.

Norris is uncomfortable with his brakes at Monza.

Given he’s well outside of the fastest for now, the pressure is on him to make Q3.

The two Aston Martins are out, along with Yuki Tsunoda, Alex Albon, Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Perez.

Q2 awaits, with Gasly fastest - aiming for what would be his first pole.

Alonso, meanwhile, has wirthdrawn from the session. Things going wrong for the veteran, who must have no other hobbies.

FOUR MINUTES TO GO IN Q1TOP 6 ⬆️Gasly VerstappenColapintoAntonelliRussellHamiltonBOTTOM 6 ⬇️Hulkenberg AlbonBottasAlonsoStrollPerez#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/BYdYjrjtnu

Pierre Gasly takes his Alpine for a spin. He is now fastest, with Verstappen second, and Colapinto bookending the Dutchman.

Antonelli and then Russell next, with the stricken Antonelli likely to give his colleague a tow.

The Red Bull man is 0.216s clear of Hamilton, with Piastri just behind.

No surprising stragglers just yet, but 11 minutes to go of this section.

We’ve 16 minutes left, and some cars are finally coming out to do battle.

18 minutes ahead before the final two rounds. Nobody is doing anything. As they say in football: tactically fascinating.

Monza paddock is absolutely sweltering. 33.8C out here. I just passed Fabio Capello on my way back to the media centre. He was speaking to Sky Sports Italia so I wasn’t able to give him my thoughts on where he went wrong at the 2010 World Cup.

Decent ding dong between Hamilton and Verstappen in practice earlier. Hopefully Hamilton is fired up for this. With Antonelli taking his grid drop at his home race, there’s a big opportunity for both Hamilton and Russell to close the gap this weekend.

The tifosi are ready 🙌It's time for qualifying at the Temple of Speed 👊#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/jeiTcb8Ij2

The cars will soon be out on the track, and we’ll have reports of their progress.

There are actually times when affection for a car company makes sense, despite what I said earlier.

Sound on... listen to the reception for Charles and Lewis ❤️#F1 #ItalianGP @ScuderiaFerrari pic.twitter.com/kk6BvA1UdC

As touched on earlier, Lewis Hamilton has to hope Charles Leclerc will work with him.

The Monegasque (look it up) is the junior partner at this point, whether he wants to be or not. That might not make him entirely delighted, but he can tow the British driver around and give him a launch for fast laps, if he’s feeling helpful.

Everyone now has access to PowerPoint, which means we all now have to have, “learnings.”

Imagine if someone you met in real life said that to you.

3 hours of laps and learnings done.#ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/GTvOvL5L5M

Given Antonelli is still one of the quickest on the track, it would be no surprise if he can at least make the top 10.

Favourable accidents and yellow flags might offer up more opportunities, too, but both Hamilton and Russell need to strike while they have such a clear advantage.

George Russell tops Lewis Hamilton in final practice in Monza 🇮🇹💪 pic.twitter.com/jxIO13aRX6

I’m as big a fan of F1 as the next man, assuming the next man quite likes F1, but there is something strange about supporting a car company, isn’t there?

🇮🇹 Sentendo il calore dell'Italia! 🥰🇬🇧 Feeling the warmth of Italy! 🥰 pic.twitter.com/ze6Ww1Z0zx

The session starts in around 40 minutes, so drivers are on their Gameboys and Instagram, and reading the weekend edition of The Telegraph.

Words we live by, this weekend and always ❤️ pic.twitter.com/0QoGlpzOHI

Here’s our interview with Alex Albon about a grim weekend at Monza.

“Alex Albon remembers the 2022 Italian Grand Prix well. He had been looking forward to it. ‘We had a car which was good down the straights that year so I was quite excited to be going to Monza,” the Williams driver recalls, a little wistfully.

‘We did FP1 and FP2 and sure enough we were quick so I was like: ‘This is going to be a good weekend.’

“Albon could not have been more wrong. He remembers waking at around 1am that night and being unable to get back to sleep.

“What happened next was the stuff of nightmares. Albon called the doctor, was diagnosed with appendicitis, sent to San Gerardo Hospital in Monza for surgery, only to suffer an unexpected complication during the procedure, which resulted in acute respiratory failure.”

He shares the joint record with Michael Schumacher for most wins at Monza.

Schumacher, a Ferrari legend, ended his career with five. Hamilton has the same.

Sport loves an emotional link to records, so be prepared for this to become a big moment.

Five wins apiece for Michael and Lewis 🖐#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/j10lMygYft

The Italian team are bringing an upgrade engine to Monza for the weekend.

Hamilton would desperately love to go out at the top after what is a remarkable return to decent form after some years of desperate struggle.

With Antonelli possibly out of the running this weekend, this is the chance to change the - *spits in self-scorn* - narrative.

Russell might have incurred a penalty if he had done this in qualifying.

The Mercedes man blocked Oscar Piastri’s run at a corner, forcing some heavy braking from his rival.

Thankfully, Piastri ducked out, and thankfully for Russell, he’s not facing censure.

A near miss for Oscar Piastri! 😬 pic.twitter.com/y6UMu8wIDM

Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton go racing! 🍿 pic.twitter.com/Zs8u8h4XoT

The former world champion is still looking for more from his car.

“Just looking at the deltas there, I was losing something like 0.6secs to George on the straights, which is something we need to look into,” Hamilton said yesterday, before explaining his conundrum for qualifying, suggesting he may go out after Leclerc.

“The tow is everything here so [I’m] likely to be looking for the tow.”

Because Antonelli exceeded the limit of parts used for his engine, he is taking a grid penalty at Monza.

Few would entirely rule out a storming ride for him on Sunday to end up top of the pack, but is is clearly a huge task for him to score points of any kind with that disadvantage.

They are now likely both past their peaks, but Hamilton and Verstappen recalled their battles of 2021 when they clashed in practice earlier.

Verstappen was already hacked off with Hamilton for seemingly obstructing his path earlier in the session, and they almost came together in the dying moments of the session.

Hamilton needed to take the escape road at the first chicane, where the pair made contact in 2021, as Verstappen looked to slip around his occasional rival. The two of them scarcely avoided another contact.

On the radios, Verstappen claimed, “He caused that,” while Hamilton reported to Ferrari that he was, “Blocked by Max.” Perhaps there will be more aggro later.

The full list of times from earlier today.

FP3 CLASSIFICATIONRussell in the box seat heading into qualifying#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/BUrCsv92dT

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of and qualifying for the Monza Grand Prix.

Before the weekend’s racing, George Russell was, at least publicly, less than bullish about his chances in Italy.

He did, though, believe he would deliver a better showing than he had in recent weeks.

“I don’t know if we can say we’re favourites this weekend, but we probably have a greater opportunity than we’ve had in the last two races where it’s been less about the power unit and more about the chassis,” he said.

“It’s so close right now, that last tenth in qualifying can be the difference of a couple of positions, which can change the podium. Right now, I don’t know who is going to be the team to beat.”

Russell was almost a minute off winner Lando Norris of McLaren in Hungary, finishing seventh in his Mercedes. Two weeks ago, in the Netherlands, he took the last spot on the podium, with Norris winning again.

However, in the second practice session on Friday and FP3 today, Russell was quickest. He led his former colleague, Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, who was second fastest.

Red Bull’s Max Verstappen hinted at a rare good weekend as he was third fastest, about a third of a second behind Russell.

Russell, of course, needs a win soon, or he is in danger of seeing the championship run away from him entirely, as Kimi Antonelli already leads him by 59 points in the world title chase.

Perhaps psychologically just as pressing is that erstwhile teammate Hamilton is tied with Russell on 183 points, in third because he has one victory compared to Russell’s two. Slipping down the rankings could knock his confidence.

Russell has not secured pole for the last four races, so a strong showing in qualifying might be the boost he needs ahead of Sunday’s race, while Norris is looking for a pole position hat-trick.

#2036. Newcastle United consider January signing of Dion Drena Beljo after very positive scouting reports

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Dion Drena Beljo is a transfer target for Newcastle United.

The prolific Croatian striker under consideration for a January move to Tyneside.

Dion Drena Beljo has scored an astonishing 43 goals in 45 appearances for Dinamo Zagreb since joining them less than 16 months ago in July 2026.

He was only 21 when moving from club football to the Bundesliga in January 2023 and struggled with the step up in level as a young striker, only scoring five goals in 45 appearances for FC Augsburg.

After scoring 10 goals in 29 appearances for Rapid Wien in Austria, Dion Drena Beljo then getting the chance to return to Croatia and play for Dinamo Zagreb.

It has proved an inspired signing with those 43 goals in only 45 appearances.

On Sunday he scored in a 3-1 away league win over Varazdin, whilst last Thursday saw Dion Drena Beljo score as Dinano Zagreb outclassed Sunderland away from home in a 2-0 Europa League victory.

The i Paper say that their information is that Newcastle United have had Dion Drena Beljo watched across recent months and the scouting reports have fed back glowing reports.

The Dinamo Zagreb striker is now 24 and understood to be valued at around £20m.

The i Paper say that internally Newcastle United have been having intensive talks about adding a striker in the January transfer window as they look to support Matthias Jaissle after he walked into such a tough situation only 18 days before this 2026-27 season kicked off.

Newcastle United have scored only 13 goals in their 10 Premier League matches. Of their strikers, William Osula and Yoane Wissa have got one league goal each so far. The end of the summer transfer window saw the inexperienced 21-year-old Matias Fernandez-Pardo arrive, who can play as a number nine, but The i Paper report that as well as having injury issues after arriving ‘he didn’t look ready or equipped to play that role in his first four Premier League starts and might be better suited to playing in a wide role.’

The report says that the message coming out of the club is that the Newcastle United hierarchy are committed to Matthias Jaissle and that backing him with a new goalscorer in January would rubber stamp that backing. Whether that new striker/goalscorer ends up being Dion Drena Beljo remains to be seen.

Just over seven weeks to go before that January 2027 transfer window opens…

The Mag Podcast Episode 15: Fulham frustration, Newcastle United’s season report card and Relegation fears

Published: 9/11/2026 | Duration: 48 mins | Hosts: Jamie Smith, Simon Cahill & David Hutchinson

In Episode 15 of The Mag Pod, we find Jamie, Simon, and Hutch discussing their Fulham frustration. Relegation fears are debated and argued upon, with three months of the season having already passed by the trio give their Newcastle United season report card, so far.

You can play episode 15 on the audio player above or use your favourite podcast platforms including Spotify, Apple Podcasts, Amazon Music, YouTube, and Acast.

Listen to the latest episode of The Mag Pod! Join Jamie, Simon, and Hutch for unfiltered football debate.

Newcastle United’s frustrating draw at Fulham, a worrying lack of goals and an increasingly uncomfortable Premier League position dominate Episode 15 of The Mag Pod.

Jamie Smith is joined by Simon Cahill and David Hutchinson to assess the Magpies’ latest performance before delivering their quarter-season report cards, picking Newcastle’s standout players and signings, and debating whether this campaign could yet end in European qualification or a relegation battle.

The 1-1 draw at Craven Cottage provides plenty to discuss. Jacob Murphy’s spectacular strike earns praise, but Fulham’s equaliser, Harvey Barnes’ missed opportunities and Dan Burn’s controversially disallowed goal leave the lads wondering whether Newcastle have thrown away another valuable two points.

There’s particular concern about Newcastle’s attacking options. With goals proving difficult to come by, the panel questions whether the current forwards can provide what the team needs, while Hutch delivers a particularly unforgiving assessment of Harvey Barnes. Murphy’s celebration also comes under the microscope, prompting a wider discussion about supporters’ expectations and the criticism facing established members of the squad.

With ten Premier League matches played, it’s time for the first proper assessment of Newcastle United’s season. Jamie, Simon and Hutch reveal their grades, nominate their highlights, choose their best summer signings and identify their players of the season so far. Lewis Hall, Sean Steur and Lukas Horníček all feature in the conversation.

Looking ahead, the mood ranges from cautious optimism to outright pessimism. Could Newcastle recover sufficiently to challenge for European football, or is a relegation battle becoming a genuine possibility? And with Sunderland looming on the fixture list, there’s plenty of anxiety about what the coming months might bring.

There’s the usual humour, disagreements and increasingly desperate attempts to find positives, as the lads consider what supporters can realistically hope for from the rest of the season.

#2034. Sydney FC fans vow to return to the stands after ugly clash with police sparked calls for boycott

Published: 01:23 EST, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 03:07 EST, 6 November 2026

Sydney FC's active supporter group The Cove will return to the stands for the first time since October's derby, following a bitter dispute over allegations police assaulted a teenage fan and handcuffed supporter leaders before throwing them out.

The group will be back for Friday night’s match against Central Coast Mariners at Allianz Stadium in Moore Park, Sydney, after talks involving the club, NSW Police, Venues NSW and stadium security.

The Cove had threatened to boycott matches after the October 16 derby with Western Sydney Wanderers, accusing police of the 'worst policing standards' in the fixture’s 14-year history and demanding the club defend its fans.

Its return comes amid a broader push for reform, with Football Supporters Association Australia declaring that repeated reviews and weekly discussions with police are no longer sufficient.

The dispute followed a scoreless derby attended by more than 30,000 spectators at Allianz Stadium.

The Cove alleged a 17-year-old supporter was repeatedly slammed into safe-standing rails by police before being struck in the back of the head.

Sydney FC supporter group The Cove will return to Allianz Stadium following a bitter dispute over policing at October's derby

It also claimed two chant leaders, known as capos, were removed from the stadium, while five members of its leadership were handcuffed, pressed against walls and ejected without subsequently being charged.

According to the group's statement, officers later told those leadership members: 'We have nothing to legally charge you with, move on.'

The Cove alleged other supporters were also ejected without justification and accused police of antagonising fans rather than protecting them.

Daily Mail has contacted NSW Police for comment.

The Cove supporters' anger extended to Sydney FC, the APL and stadium officials, whom it challenged to intervene.

'Whilst you may stay silent and not fight for your fans, don't come crying if we don't show up,' the group said.

'Active support isn't a crime. Back your f*****g fans.'

At the centre of the dispute was The Cove's allegation that police ignored established arrangements for supporter marshals to help resolve issues in the stands.

The Cove accused police of bypassing supporter marshals during the October 16 clash with Western Sydney Wanderers

The group claimed marshalls and stadium security were overridden, with officers instead entering supporter bays and taking action without consultation.

'Nobody should be made to feel like a criminal for wanting to passionately support their club,' it said.

Sydney FC initially responded by saying it was investigating the allegations with Venues NSW, the APL and NSW Police.

A joint statement released by the club and The Cove on November 5 said subsequent discussions had produced a commitment to stronger communication, mutual respect and clearer matchday processes.

'All parties have agreed on the importance of active support to football in this country, and all believe passionate, active support and a safe matchday experience must go hand in hand,' it said.

The club thanked The Cove's leadership for its professional engagement, while the supporter group thanked Sydney FC for listening to members and standing alongside them.

The statement welcomed fans back but did not announce findings on the alleged derby incidents or specify changes to police operations.

In a subsequent Instagram post, The Cove said it wanted to ensure there was never a repeat of the round-one incidents.

The supporters will return for Sydney FC's clash with Central Coast Mariners at Allianz Stadium in Moore Park

'We are hopeful that future policing at games will reflect the efforts made by the club, and Cove leadership,' it said.

'We will be monitoring the progress closely over the coming rounds.'

The dispute has also drawn intervention from the FSAA, which says supporters elsewhere in Australia and New Zealand share concerns about excessive police and security actions.

In an open letter published on November 5, the association welcomed Western Sydney Wanderers chairman Paul Lederer's criticism of police treatment of his club's fans.

It said APL leaders shared its frustration, but argued the response needed to go beyond discussions after each incident.

'We are now at the point where reactive reviews and weekly chats with police following regular operational failures on match day are simply insufficient,' the association wrote.

The FSAA said it had recommended structural changes in 2025, including rapid response protocols, measures to prevent supporters being demonised and better communication between authorities and fan groups.

It is now pushing for a framework involving senior league management, clubs, supporter leaders, stadium operators, private security and state police commands.

#2032. What Trey Nyoni did just before Alexander Isak goal isn’t getting enough attention

Trey Nyoni’s rise at Liverpool this season has been impressive.

The youngster’s potential was obvious to Andoni Iraola’s predecessor, Arne Slot, last term, but the club rightly decided to be careful with what was an 18-year-old footballer with limited senior experience.

It’s very much a different story in 2026/27, however, with the Basque head coach having already handed the midfielder over 600 minutes of action across the Premier League, Champions League and Carabao Cup.

If three consecutive starts for Liverpool – against Chelsea, Arsenal and Fenerbahce – doesn’t prove it, you have to think that the nature of Nyoni’s introduction against Crystal Palace more or less seals the view that Nyoni has become a key player for Iraola.

The correct decision was made ahead of time to rest the former Leicester City prodigy after a flurry of games, with our player of the season last year, Dominik Szoboszlai, restored to the starting XI.

But when it came time for the Hungarian to depart the pitch due to an injury concern, it was Trey Nyoni the manager turned to at the 69th minute mark. Yes, it’s worth pointing out that senior midfielders (other than Wataru Endo) aren’t exactly running amok on the Liverpool bench at this point in time. But this felt like a trusted substitution, a body Iraola has come to rely on, rather than one that just had to be made.

The assist credit will go to Florian Wirtz for the Alexander Isak goal close to full time, but it would be remiss of us to overlook Trey Nyoni’s contribution moments before.

The teenager can be spotted cutting out a low cross from Tyrick Mitchell in the box before picking out Alexander Isak (surrounded by three Palace players) further up the pitch. The ball plays out to Victor Munoz on the right flank, and Liverpool find a Palace defence in absolute disarray.

Isak strikes late on 💪🇸🇪 pic.twitter.com/J2fHbXlZyD

It’s not a fancy crossfield pass or Hollywood Gerrard ball, but there’s intention behind it, and it’s a positive use of the ball to help kickstart a Liverpool counter. Exactly what Andoni Iraola wants to see his midfielders doing at Liverpool on a frequent basis.

Ultimately, it’s so encouraging to see Nyoni continuing to be impactful in games even when he’s coming on, effectively, to see things out.

#2029. ‘I feel healthy, 120 per cent’ Newcastle United star gives update on comeback from injury

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Newcastle United star Anthony Elanga has given an update on his comeback from injury.

The winger picked up an injury back in September during a Newcastle United training session and has now revealed to media in Sweden: “It was an injury that was a little difficult to identify, it was in the groin, but I came back faster than anyone thought.”

It was just ahead of kick-off on 14 September 2026 away against Leeds at Elland Road that we found out Anthony Elanga had picked up a mystery injury.

Elanga having helped United to an excellent start to the season with three wins and two draws in the opening five games, with the Sweden star scoring in the Premier League matches against both Liverpool and Tottenham.

A ridiculous number of injuries for Matthias Jaissle to cope with so early in the season, as days after that defeat at Leeds, the Newcastle United boss had nine players ruled out for the Hull match which United won 2-1.

There was talk of Anthony Elanga potentially missing a large part of the season but instead he only two more matches after that Hull one.

A day less than six weeks after missing the Leeds match, Elanga playing the final 13 minutes of the win at Palace, then the second half at Everton in the Carabao Cup, first 76 minutes at home to Everton in the Premier League, last five minutes at Fulham.

Anthony Elanga telling Fotbollskanalen: “I took care of myself very well. I ate well, I rest well. The medical team at my club team was very good with me and the cooperation with my own team that I work with off the pitch [was good]. It was a strange injury and I’m just happy to be back.”

Anthony Elanga asked if he is still feeling the injury today: “Nothing. I now feel healthy, 120 per cent. I’m back now and…it is about getting into the same momentum that I had at the start of the season. Now I’m happy to be here, back with the national team, and building on that momentum.”

Anthony Elanga missed the Nations League matches in the last international window with Sweden but is now part of the squad that will face Bosnia-Herzegovina and Poland.

Then in response to that confirmation of the Newcastle United match decision, this Sunderland fans statement from RAWA (Red And White Army): ‘It would seem Northumbria Police will not reassess their decision to impose a full bubble trip for the Tyne–Wear derby and the reality of this decision kicks in. Despite all of this, Northumbria Police have refused to reconsider. We still have not seen a convincing explanation for why a bubble is needed. We at RAWA are gutted for the travelling Sunderland fans who will be impacted by this, and we have no doubt that these arrangements will be reciprocated for Newcastle fans for the return fixture. Where do we go from here?’

#2027. “I’m really upset” – One thing hugely annoyed Andoni Iraola despite Liverpool win on Sunday

Andoni Iraola was left ‘really upset’ after Liverpool’s win over Crystal Palace on Sunday despite the positive, morale-boosting result for his team.

Having begun November with defeats to Arsenal and Fenerbahce, the Reds went to Selhurst Park in search of a pick-me-up in their final game prior to the international window, and they duly got in the form of a 3-1 victory.

Goals from Alexis Mac Allister, Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak had the points secured well before a stoppage-time penalty when, in a clash of heads between Milos Kerkez and Dario Osorio, the Hungarian was deemed to be the perpetrator and referee Tony Harrington pointed to the spot.

Eddie Nketiah converted from 12 yards to deny Liverpool a fifth Premier League clean sheet of the campaign, and speaking to Sky Sports shortly after the final whistle, Iraola’s frustration over the awarding of the penalty was clear.

The Basque said: “I’m very upset [with] what they are calling in our box penalties, and the ones they’re not calling in the other box. I know that we are 3-0, it’s the 95th minute, but I’m very upset.

“It’s a head-to-head but even Osorio’s head, after touching the ball, is the one going to Milos. It’s not Milos to Osorio. A clash of heads.

“OK, you can say 3-0, 95 minutes, nothing happens, but for me there is more than this. There is more because it’s not the first time this season and you compare and I’m really upset, yes.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Thankfully the decision came at a point in the match where it had no bearing on the overall result, although we can still see why it put a dampener on the victory for Iraola.

To us, it seemed like a 50-50 contest between Kerkez and Osorio, with both players making a genuine attempt to win the ball and unfortunate to have clashed heads – most importantly, both were fine after the collision.

Harrington’s call didn’t have any major impact in the overall context of the day, but we take the Liverpool head coach’s point about the apparent inconsistency in terms of what referees deem to be a penalty and what they don’t.

There was certainly a far stronger case for a spot kick in our defeat to Arsenal last weekend when Jurrien Timber blatantly tugged Isak’s shirt inside the box, but somehow none of the officials on duty thought it was a foul.

It didn’t hurt the Reds yesterday, but hopefully on another occasion where there’s a stoppage-time penalty given in a game which is in the balance, we won’t end up having to talk about Iraola’s side being wronged by the referee and VAR.

#2026. Exclusive: Insider’s Verdict On ‘Brighton Star To West Ham’ Transfer Claim

One player who was reportedly linked with a move to West Ham United during the summer transfer window was Brighton & Hove Albion winger Amario Cozier-Duberry.

The 21-year-old joined Middlesbrough on a season-long loan after signing a new three-year contract with the Seagulls earlier this summer.

Cozier-Duberry has made an impressive start to life at the Riverside Stadium, registering three goals and five assists in just ten league appearances.

West Ham strengthened their wide options following the departure of Crysencio Summerville, bringing in Edvin Austbø and Manor Solomon. However, as Claret & Hugh can exclusively reveal, reports suggesting the Hammers submitted either a loan or permanent offer for Cozier-Duberry were inaccurate.

When approached for clarification, a trusted transfer source provided a brief but unequivocal response: “Not true.”

West Ham settled on Austbø – and appear to have done pretty well by signing the up and coming young winger

The winger attracted interest from several clubs during the summer, including Rangers, as uncertainty surrounded his future at Brighton following the club’s reported £21 million investment in Zadock Yohanna.

Before joining Middlesbrough, Cozier-Duberry enjoyed an outstanding loan spell with Bolton Wanderers in League One last season. He scored 11 goals and contributed 13 assists, underlining his reputation as one of the country’s most promising young attacking talents.

At West Ham, Manor Solomon has experienced a mixed start to his spell in east London, while Austbø has already chipped in with two goals and two assists despite largely being used as a substitute.

It will be fascinating to see how Cozier-Duberry’s loan campaign at Middlesbrough develops over the course of the season. However, any suggestion that he was close to wearing a claret-and-blue shirt appears to be wide of the mark.

#2025. West Ham fans’ furious reaction raises an uncomfortable question

As the Hammers subsided to their first away defeat in the Championship, long suffering supporters, who’d undertaken the 480 mile round trip to be served up a pretty spineless team performance, decided to let their team have it with both barrels.

After last week’s displeasure culminating an Hammers fans singing ‘sacked in the morning’ to their own manager, this weekend brought the players into the crosshairs as the next logical target for their ire.

..With Nuno Espirito Santo out of the job and with Scott Parker just 72 hours in, the 7,500+ travelling fans turned on their stars.

Under no illusions after the result – and the away fans’ response – yesterday: Scott Parker

..As well as booing their own goal keeper pretty much throughout, if the reports on the radio were correct.

Traditionalists will likely be aghast at the thought of fans undermining their own team in this manner, whilst those who participated no doubt feel it was the only way to show their contempt for the perceived lack of commitment and effort which those eleven representatives  of the Claret and Blue heritage displayed.

Not to mention the hundreds of pounds it costs each supporter, every game, merely to arrive at the turnstiles in support of our club. But is it the ‘right’ thing to do?

For me – it’s a no. I started attending games with my son when he was ten years old and however bad it got (it was pretty dire in that season of 2003-4) we never left early, never booed our own players (Luis Boa Morte excepted, I must confess to once letting my frustration with his indolence bubble over) and always, always applauded those who’d put in a shift, regardless of outcome. And I’d not even heard ‘you’re not fit to wear the shirt‘ sung by West Ham fans in my couple of decades’ worth of attending games.

I just don’t see it helping team morale or positively influencing the final outcome. Which is, after all, the point of ‘supporters’.

Giving ‘The Sun’ another gleeful headline to point out our sufferings sticks in my throat too.

But don’t get me wrong, each has absolutely the right to their own response. Just don’t see it helping is all.

To the negatives, support our team or push off. I have attended since 58. We never had the Russian or Mafia money but it is still our club. Great memories of neighbours and friends who played for the club. Most of our players did their best, including youngsters but we need a strong striker and physical keeper.

been trying to get more away tickets, anyone who doesn’t want to go and watch the away games, step aside there’s plenty who want to go but can’t get tickets….

Booing is not motivational we have a new manager who has seemingly had very limited time with the squad he needs a chance to see what he can do and Booing is not helping. The club has had many problems for some time. The situation is frustrating from now on we have to get behind the team.

How can anyone be surprised. Week after week watching the same old dross . A centre back who would struggle to get a game in a pub team and a goalkeeper who is totally useless. New manager comes in and picks them both AGAIN!! How many times do Kilman and Hermansen have to lose us games before someone wises up .

Considering how much it costs to travel to, & to get into, games – & the grossly excessive salaries the players receive – I consider that the supporters have every right to criticise what they see from the players on the pitch. It could be counter-productive, in that it upsets the players’ mindsets & effort, but what about the mindsets of those who, at least partially, pay their salaries. I don’t like to see the players get booed etc., but the supporters do have the right to express their opinions – just as they do when they cheer the players. These are professional players & yet they continue to serve up displays which are not even worthy of amateurs – who don’t get paid obscene salaries & do it for the love of the game. They should take the supporters’ criticisms as an incentive to raise their game & make an extra effort for , what could be described as, their employers.

I don’t agree with these chants, but if you are a paying customer, it is your right I suppose. All I will say is, if Scott Parker wasn’t aware of the size of the job he has signed up for, he certainly does now. And when it comes to the goalkeeping situation, Hermandsen reminds me of Mervyn Day, a very good young keeper who came through the youth ranks, which we all really like. But through a series of unfortunate incidents, like being lobbed from forty yards on a couple of occasions, he had been reduced to a rabbit in the headlights, his nerve completely shot. John Lyall realising that in his current state of mind he wouldn’t be good enough to take us forward, did the extremely unkind but completely necessary act of removing him from the team, and go out and break the world record for Phil Parkes, and that didn’t work out to badly did it? Harsh, absolutely, but football doesn’t exist on seniment, difficult choices sometimes have to be made. Mr Parker has been around the game long enough to be well aware of this, and I don’t think he will hesitate to do whatever is required to fix this and other positions.

You clearly don’t go to many away games. It also happened at Cardiff away and Leeds away last season.

I think our fans are very poor compared to other clubs who shout and sing all the way through the game. Look at the Lincoln supporters who were all singing at 6-0 down. Our ground is like a morgue until we score and also if we go behind. Leaving before the end is the pits, when we are down we need more support than ever

You’ve obviously never tried to get out of the London Stadium.

This is the worst squad of players and I’ve been watching for 60 years!! We are being beaten or draw with opposition who are extremely average BUT work hard for each other for 90 minutes and we pass the ball from side to side and backwards with zero creativity, zero pace and it’s abysmal. 100% these players need to be booed and criticized, they are pathetic, Bowen included!!

The team isn’t perfect but it’s certainly not spineless. Just look at the number of games we have come from behind in. Lacking the ability to control games, absolutely. Lacking the right balance, definitely. Lacking experience in a number of areas, certainly. It is a difficult time for sure. It affects every part of our lives but we must stick together and trust in the new head coach. He’ll make some wrong decisions but get more right. Most of us won’t agree with many of them but they are not our decisions to make. Supporting is what we are here for. You may not feel the players have earned unconditional support but we all know they need it.

I attended the WBA game with a respectful WBA fan and he was genuinely shocked at fans leaving on 70 mins and booing. He’s the same age as me (mid 40s) and couldn’t get his head round it.

I’ve been going since 87/88 so this season is like a party in the park compared to some of the dross I’ve seen. It’ll have to get pretty bad for me to boo the players.

Won’t lie I’ve boo’d a few of the managers in the past and obviously the board. Not sure I can sit there boo’ing and shouting the c bomb for 90 mins like the holiday supporter behind me the other day. Can’t waste the energy caring that much anymore or risking a heart attack.

I have trouble understanding the attitudes of an awful lot of our supporters these days. I know we’re all entitled to our opinions, and how we react is pretty subjective, but why travel all the way to Blackburn just to express vitriol when the result doesn’t go your way? As someone that has been going since 1968, and for a long period seldom missed a game, home or away, this attitude is a relatively recent phenomenon. Is it linked to a sense of entitlement that seems to be prevalent in society these days? It certainly doesn’t improve the matchday experience. I’ve witnessed far worse teams and performances that Saturday’s one that have never provoked the sort of response I’m stunned came from West Ham supporters. Who, exactly, wasn’t ‘fit to wear the shirt’? Jarrod Bowen? Ezra Myers? That chant isn’t one size fits all, you know. And let’s be honest. For the overwhelming majority of the game, West Ham were camped in the Blackburn half faced with 2 banks of 5 defending their goal. A couple of good saves by their keeper stopped us, and if Bowen’s header had been 2 inches to the left the result would probably have been very different.

The trouble with the chant is all the players are put in the same boat. My view Kilman and the goalkeeper were poor and probably deserved it. Up front we want a centre forward, Championship is just not Tatty’s game Peroe needs someone playing with him and we haven’t got anyone who can play the target man. Scott hasn’t had a chance to change things yet and Myers was probably the best player on the pitch for us. The chants left the players with no doubt how we all feel, now if the team come out next game and start on the front foot get behind them. You can’t do one without the other!

Bowen and Myers’s to name but two. Ive 12 other names of players who weren’t fit to wear the shirt yesterday if you want them? Or save me the trouble and check the team sheet. Every one was rubbish, no exception. Time we stopped making excuses and remember if it quacks it is a duck, and our squad is as bad as I’ve seen in 40 years. Overpaid and overrated.

I love it these players have got away with it for to long

Totally agree, how can it do anything but make the performance worse?

Spot on. My thoughts entirely. Our goalkeeper will also be shot to pieces with all the criticism.

Or perhaps that goalkeeper is just remarkably incapable of saving anything! Look at the second goal he didn’t even bother moving he just ushered the ball into our net. As for the idea muted in the article that we haven’t sung you’re not fit to wear the shirt before I have to ask where has the author been as we’ve sung that throughout the years. I really love the rewriting of history that goes on it makes me laugh, Allan McKnight, David Kelly, Alex bunbury, Mike small, Gary strodder, Lee chapman, rigobert song and many others in the 80s and 90s may disagree as they heard that sung at them on many occasions. The travelling fans deserve far better than the rubbish that’s being served up and I’m surprised so many fans appear to defend the dross on display, preferring to batter the fans as the underachieving prima Donna’s trudge around yet again

I no stats don’t tell the whole story, but they don’t scream out “spineless” to me. It looks more like good control of the game, chances made and missed then being caught on the break. Perhaps someone who was there can put me straight if I am mistaken

I wasn’t there but having watched The Irons since the 1970s all I can say is players, managers and owners come and go, only the fans remain. ‘Boing the team’? If they deserve it, why not? It is a privilege to play for West Ham. They should act like it and play like their lives depend on it. Killman looks as though he’s drugged and kidnapped and is not a footballer at all. No, if the team were booed I’m sure they deserved it. They’ll get a standing ovsiif they loose… so long as they try.

I wasn’t there but having watched The Irons since the 1970s all I can say is players, managers and owners come and go, only the fans remain. ‘Boing the team’? If they deserve it, why not? It is a privilege to play for West Ham. They should act like it and play like their lives depend on it. Killman looks as though he’s drugged and kidnapped and is not a footballer at all. #2024. Didier Deschamps 'doesn't want Manchester United job': Blow for Sir Jim Ratcliffe as unemployed former France boss appears hesitant to replace under-fire Michael Carrick

Published: 04:37 EST, 6 November 2026 | Updated: 04:37 EST, 6 November 2026

Manchester United have suffered a road bump in sounding out potential replacements for Michael Carrick – as Didier Deschamps reportedly doesn't want the gig.

Deschamps, who left the France job after 14 years following the World Cup, has told the club he is uninterested according to the Daily Mirror.

Carrick remains in post but his bosses have been privately talking to possible successors for weeks after an abysmal start to the season which has left them 17th in the Premier League.

Eddie Howe, Fabian Hurzeler, Unai Emery and Antonio Conte have all come up on the shortlist, with the international break this month seen as an ideal time for managerial changes across the league.

Deschamps appealed to United because of his immediate availability and lack of a compensation fee, but is in no rush to take a job and snubbed their advance.

After a glittering career as a player, he has won the World Cup managing France, lifted Ligue 1 with Marseille, led Monaco to a Champions League final, and got Juventus promoted back to Serie A after the Calciopoli scandal.

Didier Deschamps has reportedly told Manchester United he is not interested in the job

Michael Carrick remains in post but United have been sounding out potential replacements for weeks

Carrick's prospects of keeping the job had a boost on Tuesday as Matheus Cunha struck two late goals to produce a stunning turnaround win against Roma in the Champions League.

But he only has a clash against Aston Villa at Old Trafford on Sunday afternoon before the international break to prove to the hierarchy that he should keep his job.

That comeback against Roma stopped a rot which has been spreading for weeks. United were on the verge of going ten games without a win, a run unprecedented in the club's history.

They have reached a nadir in recent weeks after batterings by Como and Bournemouth – the latter at Old Trafford, no less – while players have been openly mutinous.

Bruno Fernandes publicly criticised Carrick's tactics after the 4-1 defeat at Como, leading to Carrick benching him for the next game against Bournemouth.

And Lisandro Martinez has singled out director of football Jason Wilcox over United's transfer activity, suggesting the squad was left short on quality after the transfer window.

Were Carrick to go, it is unclear who would replace him.

Emery is open to signing a new deal with Aston Villa which would take him to close to a decade at the club, and held a meeting with club chiefs on Wednesday.

Hurzeler does not have a release clause in his Brighton contract and so would require enormous compensation. There is well-placed scepticism as to whether any move would even be remotely possible, regardless of how well liked he is inside Old Trafford.

Nagelsmann and Conte are both out of work and the latter has previously indicated that he would like the challenge of restoring a fallen giant to glory.
